newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew puts robot arm to work.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew puts robot arm to work.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Discovery, circling Earth 185 miles (296 km) up, conducted a test on Monday by flexing the muscles of a Japanese prototype space station robot arm.

Although the movements of the multi-jointed 5 ft (1.6 metre) arm were frequently stalled by an overly sensitive safety system, the check went well, according to Masanori Magatomo of the Japanese space agency.
During its orbital workout, the dextrous arm unbolted a simulated electronics box and opened and closed doors.
The $100 million mechanical marvel is a prototype of an arm that will tend to experiments mounted on the exterior of a Japanese laboratory at the planned International Space Station.
"It's designed to do very delicate tasks and it's working quite well so far," Discovery crewman Robert Curbeam said during a radio interview on Monday.
The astronauts' day began early with a call from mission control. The crew was woken after an experiment in the shuttle cargo bay malfunctioned leaving a laser beam stuck on.
"Sorry to wake you up," mission control's Marc Garneau told shuttle skipper Curt Brown.
"No problem, we're up here to help out," the four-time space flier replied.
Flight controllers had feared the laser light could interfere with other experiments aboard the shuttle. The faulty experiment was quickly reset and began recording data again.
The 11-day mission features 24 major experiments, spanning the fields of medical research, astronomy and environmental monitoring.
A German-built satellite, released from the shuttle on Thursday and now trailing the orbiter by about 45 miles (72 kilometres), continues to gather data on the upper atmosphere.

On Sunday, scientists said an instrument aboard the free-flying satellite may have found evidence to support a theory that Earth is being bombarded by house-sized water-laden comets every few seconds.
The astronauts plan to haul the satellite back aboard Discovery on Saturday and return to Earth on Aug. 18.
